summary: For ages 11–14: build powers as repeated multiplication (tying n² to area, n³ to volume), roots as the inverse operation, and the distinction between an exact surd (√2, √20) and its never-settling decimal approximation. Fluency with power sequences (powers of 2, 3, 4, 5) and correct order-of-operations handling of powers support the core conceptual work.
misconceptions: Reading n² as n×2 and n³ as n×3 (multiplying by the exponent instead of repeated multiplication)
Believing a rounded decimal equals the root (1.414 = √2) rather than approximating it
Assuming every number has a 'nice' exact root, or that √ always yields a whole number
Confusing square and cube (or their roots), especially in volume/area contexts
Mishandling powers in BIDMAS — evaluating left-to-right rather than powers before ×/÷

activities.title: Power/root workbench on arrays
steps: Set a base and exponent: pick base 3, exponent 2, and watch a 3×3 square fill in reading area = 9; raise the exponent (e.g. to 4) and see a factor string assemble, 3×3×3×3 = 81 (that is 3⁴).
Switch to root mode: given an area of 49, resize a square until it fits exactly — side 7 — and record √49 = 7.
Given an area of 20, try to square off a whole-number side; observe that no whole side fits, the exact label √20 stays pinned, and a decimal read-out ticks 4.47…, 4.472… without ever landing.
State in your own words why √20 is the exact value while the decimal is only ever an approximation.
activities.insight: A power is repeated multiplication (not base × exponent); a root is the inverse that recovers the side/edge; and for non-perfect roots the surd is the exact value while the decimal only approximates it, never catching up.

activities.title: Build a cube to feel n³ as volume
steps: Stack unit cubes into an n×n×n cube (e.g. a 4×4×4 cube) and count the total to feel n³ as a volume.
Reverse the task: given a volume such as 64, find the edge length to establish ∛64 = 4.
Compare: say whether ∛64 is exact and how that differs from √2.
activities.insight: Cube numbers and cube roots have a genuine three-dimensional meaning (volume and edge), and perfect cubes give exact roots while numbers like 2 do not.

activities.title: Power-sequence reference wall
steps: Reveal values on a powers-of-2, 3, 4 and 5 wall, reading each value alongside its factor string (e.g. 2⁵ = 2×2×2×2×2 = 32, 5³ = 5×5×5 = 125).
Use the wall to recognise landmark powers (powers of 2 up to 2¹⁰, powers of 3 up to 3⁵, powers of 4 up to 4⁵ and powers of 5 up to 5⁴) on sight.
Spot which listed values are perfect squares or perfect cubes.
activities.insight: Key power sequences become recognisable landmarks that speed recall and help judge whether a root is likely to be exact.

activities.title: Consolidation: evaluate and classify
steps: Match bases to their power-sequence landmarks (e.g. 3 → 9, 27, 81).
Decide which of √25, √20, √9 is NOT exact, and explain why.
Evaluate a mixed expression such as 3 + 2² and explain the order used.
activities.insight: Once meaning is built, learners can evaluate powers and roots fluently, identify exact versus approximate roots, and apply order of operations correctly.

activities.title: Justify why √2 ≠ 1.414
steps: Discuss and answer: does 1.414 equal √2? Square 1.41 (= 1.9881) and 1.414 (= 1.999396) and report whether either hits 2.
Explain why no terminating decimal can equal √2, and what the exact value is.
activities.insight: √2 is irrational: its decimal never terminates or repeats, so any decimal is only an approximation and the exact value remains the surd √2.

checkQuestion: Work these on paper, showing what you do. (1) Calculate 4³. (2) Find √49 and ∛64. (3) Is √2 an exact number you can write down fully, or an approximation? Explain.
checkAnswer: (1) 64 (4×4×4). (2) √49 = 7, ∛64 = 4. (3) √2 is irrational — its decimal (1.41421…) never terminates or repeats, so 1.41 is only an approximation; the exact value stays written as √2.
